democracy-best.rationale: In the same Journal entry (14 March 1826) he warned that grinding down Scottish peculiarities would throw the country 'into a state in which it will be universally turned to democracy', which he called 'a very dangerous North British neighbourhood'; in March 1831 he drew up an address 'reprobatory of the Bill' for parliamentary reform.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: In his Life of Napoleon (1827) he wrote that the royalists of 1789 should have joined those who wished 'to infuse into [monarchy] the spirit of rational liberty, and to place Louis in such a situation as should have ensured him the safe and honourable station of a limited monarch, though it deprived him of the powers of a despot', and that Buonaparte 'would have consulted even his own interest better' by choosing 'to be the head of a well-regulated and limited monarchy' than a despotism. A limited monarch with reserved rights is not purely ceremonial.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: In his Journal of 14 March 1826, on his Letters of Malachi Malagrowther, he wrote that ministers 'are gradually destroying what remains of nationality' in Scotland and that 'loosening and grinding down all those peculiarities which distinguished us as Scotsmen' would be dangerous; he wrote the letters 'to put the people of Scotland on their guard'.

region-keeps-system.rationale: In his Letter of 1826 he defended the Scottish banking system, in which Scottish banks issue their own small notes, as having 'been attended with the greatest advantage to the country', and objected to 'the apparent hostility towards our municipal institutions... tending to force and wrench them into a similarity with those of England'; in his Second Letter he explained the guards that protect the Scottish paper currency and asked that Scottish arrangements guaranteed in the Union be left alone.

rehabilitation.rationale: In his Journal of 20 February 1826, after a visit from a prison reformer, he wrote: 'I do not see the propriety of making them dandy places of detention. They should be a place of punishment, and that can hardly be if men are lodged better, and fed better, than when they are at large', adding that he had 'some distrust of the fanaticism--even of philanthropy'.

treaties-binding.rationale: In his Second Letter of Malachi Malagrowther (1826) he wrote that 'we have a system of laws peculiar to us, secured by treaties', that English statesmen forget what 'the weaker party in a national treaty' remembers, and called the proposed measure on Scottish bank notes 'unauthorized by justice, conducted without regard to the faith of treaties, and contrary to our national privileges'; he urged Scottish members of Parliament to unite against it as a breach of the Articles of Union.

notes: A first audit from the one Scott text in the local Project Gutenberg library, his Journal, read by theme (prisons, Scottish nationality, parliamentary reform, Catholic emancipation, religion). Six statements answered. From the Gutenberg texts, the Journal and volumes I-II of the Life of Napoleon are cited; the other volumes of the Napoleon, the Letters on Demonology, the editions and the novels and poems are declined in booksNotUsed (characters' views in the fiction are not his). The first two Letters of Malachi Malagrowther (1826, Internet Archive) are read by theme and cited (the third letter, a dialogue on the currency, was scanned by theme and repeats the argument). The uncertainty rule is not met.
